chunks.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment — working draft

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub reads police records and produces analysis over them: crime trend
forecasts, geographic hotspots, case-pendency projections, link analysis between
people and cases, and four person-level risk and outcome scores.

Every output is decision support. Nothing the system produces authorises an action
against an individual, and no threshold triggers anything automatically — each one
orders a queue for a person to work. This is a design constraint, stated in
`GOVERNANCE.md` and reflected in the code, not an aspiration.

**Current processing state:** the deployed corpus is *synthetic*. No real police
record has been processed. That fact bounds every risk rating below and must be
re-read when it changes.
chunks.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment — working draft › 1. What the system does

chunks.text:
Thirty-eight tables. The categories that carry personal data:

| Category | Examples | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Accused and offender identity | Name, age, gender, address, aliases, photograph reference, fingerprint identifier | **High** — criminal-history data, special category under most regimes |
| Victim identity | Name, age, gender, contact, relationship to accused | **High** |
| Criminal history | Prior cases, arrests, chargesheets, convictions, acquittals, rowdy-sheeter and history-sheeter flags | **High** |
| Case detail | FIR narrative, crime type, location, severity, witness counts | **High** — narratives are free text and may contain anything |
| Officer records | Name, rank, station, caseload | Moderate — employment data |
| Derived assessments | Conviction likelihood, recidivism risk band, case-closure and pendency projections | **High** — inferences about named individuals |
| Access records | Who viewed which person's file, when, and the reason given | Moderate — employment/conduct data |

Note the last two rows. The system does not only *hold* personal data, it **creates**
it: a risk band attached to a named person is new personal data about them, and is
treated as such throughout — it is disclosable, contestable, and erasable.
chunks.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment — working draft › 2. Personal data processed

chunks.text:
The copilot and agent features send prompt text to **Groq** (`api.groq.com`) and
**NVIDIA** (`integrate.api.nvidia.com`), both outside India and outside the
authority's control. This is the single point where personal data leaves the
deployment.

**Control in place:** `privacy.py` replaces person names with stable aliases before
any prompt is built, and restores them in the reply on the way back. The provider
receives the structure of the question and pseudonymised identifiers.

**Residual risk, stated plainly:** pseudonymisation is not anonymisation. A free-text
FIR narrative can identify a person without naming them — an address, a vehicle, an
unusual offence in a small district. Alias mapping does not remove that, and no
automated check can reliably detect it.

**[AUTHORITY]** must decide whether third-party LLM inference is permitted at all
against real records, and if so under what contractual terms (retention by the
provider, training use, jurisdiction). If it is not permitted, the copilot must be
disabled or pointed at a self-hosted model; the code path is a single configuration
change, and the rest of the platform functions without it.

chunks.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment — working draft › 6. Data principal rights

chunks.text:
**[AUTHORITY]**

This section requires a determination that cannot be made from the code: whether each
category of processing is necessary for the stated policing purpose, and whether the
same outcome could be achieved with less personal data. The system's own position is
recorded in `GOVERNANCE.md` — that its outputs order queues rather than authorise
actions — but whether that processing is proportionate is a decision for the data
fiduciary.

Points that should inform it:

* Person-level risk scoring is the most intrusive processing here and the least
 accurate. The registry publishes where each model fails to beat a trivial baseline;
 that evidence should be read before deciding these scores are necessary at all.
* Aggregate analysis — trends, hotspots, pendency — carries most of the operational
 value and far less risk. It could be deployed without the person-level scores.
* The third-party LLM flow is a convenience feature. Nothing else depends on it.

chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub

chunks.text:
**KSP IntelHub does not infer guilt.** It surfaces relationships and priorities in
recorded data for authorised operational review.

Everything below follows from that sentence.

---
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › The principle

chunks.text:
Risk scores, conviction outlooks, link predictions and hotspot zones are decision
support for allocating attention. None of it is evidence, and none of it may be
presented to a court as such.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 1. No output is evidence

chunks.text:
Person-level probabilities are calibrated and never display 0% or 100%. Where a model
is outside its supported range — a case older than its observation grid — the platform
**refuses to score it** rather than extrapolating, and reports how much of the docket
it declined.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 2. Nothing is stated as certainty

chunks.text:
Every threshold in the model cards orders a queue for a person to work. None of them
authorises an action against an individual. A human decision sits between every score
and every consequence.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 3. No output triggers an action automatically

chunks.text:
Each model publishes its split dates, baselines, calibration curve, feature
importances and the warnings its own training run raised. Every score handed to a
person is logged, every published model keeps its previous versions so a bad one can
be rolled back, and `/models/drift` reports how far the current population has moved
from the one each model learned on — naming the models it cannot monitor and why,
rather than omitting them so that silence reads as safety. The composite District
Operational Risk Index and the dispatch staffing recommendation publish their weights
and per-component arithmetic — a composite score with no visible arithmetic is the
easiest artefact in this domain to produce and the hardest to defend.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 4. Every number is traceable

chunks.text:
Every model is reported next to the trivial baseline it has to beat, **including where
it fails to**. The crime forecast still ties a 4-week moving average, and the registry
says so on the page rather than in a footnote.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 5. Measured against doing nothing

chunks.text:
Trial-outcome accuracy is broken out by age band and gender, so a model that works
overall but fails a subgroup cannot pass unnoticed. A widening gap is a stop
condition, not a note.

---
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Six constraints › 6. Subgroup performance is checked

chunks.text:
Automated assessment without a route to challenge it is the failure mode every
framework for this exists to prevent. Three things are needed and all three exist:

* **Disclosure.** `GET /api/subject-report/ ` (supervisor-only, audited) assembles
 everything the system holds and asserts about one person: every score with its date,
 the model's own stated limits and out-of-scope uses, who accessed the record and the
 reason they gave, and any challenge already raised. A person cannot contest an
 assessment they cannot see.
* **A recorded challenge.** `POST /api/contest` records one against a named subject
 and model. Grounds are required — an unreviewable challenge helps the person who
 raised it least of all — and the stated basis is kept verbatim. Resolutions are
 appended, never written over the original, so the history of a disputed assessment
 stays readable.
* **Consequence.** The contest register is consulted on the serving path, so a
 contested score reaches the officer marked wherever it is displayed. A challenge
 that changed nothing about what the officer sees would be a complaints box, not a
 control.

Filing does **not** suppress the score. Whether a challenge is well-founded is a
decision for the deploying authority, and this platform deliberately does not make it
silently — see the gaps table.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Contestability

chunks.text:
Three runtime logs accumulate personal data: who accessed whose record, what score
each person was given, and what happened to them. Each has a published retention
period with a stated justification, readable at `GET /api/retention`.

**Erasure is deliberately partial, and the reason is on the record.** A subject's
*assessments* — their scores and recorded outcomes — are erased on request. The
*access log* is not. It records who viewed their file: evidence of official conduct
rather than an assessment of the subject. A log that a subject could delete would let
anyone who improperly viewed a record destroy the proof by filing an erasure request
in that subject's name. It expires on its own three-year schedule instead, and every
erasure report states plainly what was retained and why.

The audit log is also purged at whole-file granularity rather than per entry, because
removing individual lines would break the hash chain that makes it verifiable. A
tamper-evidence control that gets rebuilt whenever it is inconvenient proves nothing.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Retention and erasure

chunks.text:
* **Aggregate surfaces are open.** District funnels, forecasts, hotspot zones and the
 model registry identify nobody, and the platform has to be legible to a reviewer
 with no credentials.
* **Person-level surfaces are gated**, and the two aggregates that contain a
 person-level block (`/stats`, `/analytics`) return that block pseudonymised rather
 than refused, so the control is visible without credentials.
* **Every person-level access is audited** — who, which subject, stated reason, result.
 Entries are hash-chained, so the log can be checked rather than trusted: any edit,
 reorder or deletion is detectable through `GET /api/audit-log/verify`. Truncation of
 the newest entries is caught against the writer's own count, not by the chain itself.
 The chain does not defend against a compromised application process, and needs
 `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` set to hold against someone with write access to the file.
 Reading the audit log is itself audited. Access without a stated reason is recorded
 as such so it is visible in review rather than indistinguishable.
* **Person names never reach the LLM providers.** The copilot injects real records into
 prompts sent to third-party services outside India; names are aliased before egress
 and restored locally in the answer.

---
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Access, audit and PII

chunks.text:
Predictive policing systems carry a documented risk of entrenching the patterns in
their own training records: enforcement concentrates where past enforcement was
recorded, which generates the very data that justifies concentrating there. A hotspot
is a property of *recorded incidents*, and recorded incidents reflect where officers
have previously been sent.

Nothing in this platform is exempt from that. It is built to be audited — which is why
the registry publishes what each model failed at alongside what it achieved, and why
the hotspot card asks whether zones re-appear in the same places every cycle.

---
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › The feedback-loop risk

chunks.text: Stated because their absence is a gap, not an oversight.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Known gaps

chunks.text:
| Gap | Status |
|---|---|
| **Retention enforcement between restarts** | The schedule is published with its justification (`GET /api/retention`); purge and erasure are implemented and tested; and a retention pass runs **on every container start** when `RETENTION_ENFORCE=1`, logging the backlog either way. AppSail has no scheduler, so a restart is the only recurring event this application can hook — a long-lived container will hold past-retention entries until it next restarts or an operator calls the endpoint. |
| **Adjudicating a challenge** | Challenges are recorded, disclosed and marked on the score, but nothing decides whether one is well-founded and no challenge automatically suppresses an assessment. That is a decision for the deploying authority — this platform must not make it silently — so the process, the reviewer and the service standard all remain to be defined by whoever operates it. |
| **Operational outcomes** | The feedback loop now runs end to end, but on a **replay**, not on use. `replay_outcomes.py` scores the held-out window through the serving artifact and feeds its real recorded results back in: 905 matured pairs for conviction, 3,343 for case closure, both consistent with published evaluation. That proves the serving path reproduces offline evaluation and that the loop works — it is **not** field performance. `realised()` reports the provenance of every
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Known gaps

chunks.text:
outcome and warns when all of them are replayed, and no prediction made in service of a real decision has been checked yet. |
| **Automatic retraining** | Manual. Drift and realised performance are both measured and reported; nothing acts on either. |
| **DPIA sign-off** | `DPIA.md` is a working draft: it records the data categories, flows, controls and residual risks that can be established from the code. The half only the deploying authority can supply — lawful basis, necessity and proportionality, consultation, sign-off — is marked `[AUTHORITY]` and left blank. chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › Known gaps

chunks.text:
**No production KSP records were used.** The corpus is CCTNS-schema-shaped *simulated*
data over the real 31 Karnataka districts, generated by a documented process in
`appsail/simulate_outcomes.py`.

Every score in this system demonstrates that the pipeline can recover structure that
was deliberately injected into the data. That is the right thing to verify before real
records exist — it validates the features, the splits and the evaluation — and it is
**not** a claim of field performance. `appsail/ml/dataset.py` is the single adapter
layer: pointing it at a real extract runs the identical pipeline with no model, metric
or endpoint changes, at which point every figure must be re-measured before it is
quoted.
chunks.title: Governance — KSP IntelHub › The data

chunks.text:
The Challenge: Moving Beyond Manual Records 

The Karnataka State Police (KSP) maintains extensive crime records capturing incidents, offenders, and victims. However, the current analytical ecosystem faces significant hurdles: 

➢ Data Silos & Manual Processes: Current records are often managed in independent silos, heavily reliant on Excel-based reporting rather than integrated, automated systems. 

➢ Lack of Advanced Analytics: There is a notable absence of AI-driven approaches, leaving deeper behavioral patterns, social interactions, and interconnected criminal networks undiscovered. 

➢ Information Gaps: The State Crime Records Bureau (SCRB) currently receives limited, fragmented information, hindering its ability to perform comprehensive state-wide analysis. 

➢ Reactive vs. Proactive: Policing remains largely reactive; without a systematic exploration of emerging trends, investigators lack the tools for proactive policing strategies and evidence-based prevention. 

The Proposed Solution: Crime Intelligence & Analytical Platform 

The goal is to develop a state-of-the-art platform that integrates sociological insights and criminological intelligence with cutting-edge technology. 

Key Capabilities:
chunks.title: PRD

chunks.text:
1. Advanced Visualization: Replace static sheets with interactive dashboards and geospatial maps to track crime clusters across districts. Some of the Data Visualization & Intelligence Report should move beyond static charts into dynamic, spatial, and relational storytelling; 

➢ District-Level Drill-down: Interactive maps allow SCRB to visualize crime patterns across districts and specific police stations.

➢ Spatiotemporal Clusters: Identification of "Crime Hotspots" by layering time of day with location, enabling proactive resource deployment. 

➢ Emerging Trend Alerts: Visual indicators (e.g., red-zone pulsing) when a specific crime category spikes in a region compared to historical averages. 

2. Criminological Network & Link Analysis 

This functionality replaces "independent silos" by visually connecting fragmented data points to reveal organized crime structures. 

➢ Relationship Mapping: A node-based visualization showing connections between suspects, victims, and recurring locations. 

➢ Repeat Offender Tracking: Visual profiles that link an individual to multiple incidents, highlighting their specific Modus Operandi (MO) across different jurisdictions. 

➢ Association Detection: Identifying hidden criminal associations that are impossible to spot in isolated Excel sheets. 

3. Sociological & AI-Driven Predictive Dashboards
chunks.title: PRD

chunks.text:
This moves the SCRB from reactive reporting to a "Strategic Intelligence Hub". 

➢ Socio-Economic Correlation: Overlays crime data with urbanization patterns, population distribution, and socio-economic indicators to understand the "why" behind the "where". 

➢ Predictive Risk Scoring: AI-driven charts that forecast potential "High-Risk" areas or emerging crime typologies based on hidden correlations. 

➢ Anomaly Detection: Visual call-outs for incidents that deviate from standard behavioral patterns, assisting investigators in linking complex cases 

4. Patter & Trend Discovery: Utilize statistical analytics to identify spatial and temporal hotspots, allowing for smarter resource deployment. 

5. Network & Behavioral Analysis: Detect connections between suspects and organized crime networks while identifying recurring Modus Operandi (MO). 

6. AI/ML-Driven Intelligence: Deploy machine learning models to identify hidden correlations, detect anomalies, and predict emerging crime risks.

chunks.title: KSP IntelHub — Karnataka State Police SCRB AI Intelligence Platform › 🚀 Live Deployment

chunks.text:
Two things AppSail needs are **gitignored**, so a clean checkout deploys
"successfully" and then refuses to start with a message that names neither:

 Execution failed. Please check the startup command or port.

* **`appsail/_vendor/`** — Catalyst does *not* install `requirements.txt`
 server-side. Dependencies must be vendored as Linux wheels. Without it the
 container cannot import flask.
* **`appsail/app-config.json`** — holds live keys, so only
 `app-config.example.json` is committed. The `command` must keep its
 `PYTHONPATH=_vendor` prefix.

**Pinned versions are load-bearing.** The registry refuses any artifact built by
a different scikit-learn than the runtime and retrains in-process instead. Seven
models retraining inside a 512 MB container exhausts it and the container
thrashes. So `requirements.txt` pins exactly what the artifacts were trained
with — Python 3.13 / scikit-learn 1.7.2 / numpy 2.2.6 / pandas 2.3.2 — and
`/serverless/api/models` shows `"source": "artifact"` for all seven when this is
right.

```bash
chunks.title: KSP IntelHub — Karnataka State Police SCRB AI Intelligence Platform › 🚀 Live Deployment › Deploying — read this first

chunks.text: python -m pip install -r appsail/requirements.txt -t appsail/_vendor --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 --python-version 3.13 --implementation cp --only-binary=:all:
chunks.title: 1. vendor Linux wheels matching the stack in app-config.json

chunks.text: cd appsail && python predeploy_check.py
chunks.title: 2. preflight — checks vendor, wheel tags, version drift and the command

chunks.text:
catalyst deploy --only appsail
catalyst deploy --only client # bump web/client-package.json version first
```

The client and the API are on **different Catalyst domains** — the client domain
does not proxy `/serverless/*` — so `web/.env.production` pins the API origin.
CORS across the two is handled by the gateway.

chunks.text:
Two shapes of response, chosen to fit what is being asked for:

| Surface | Signed out | Rationale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Forecasts, hotspots, district indices, lifecycle funnel, model registry | **Open** | Management statistics. They identify nobody, and the platform has to be legible to an evaluator with no credentials |
| Aggregates that *contain* a person-level block (`/stats`, `/analytics`) | **Pseudonymised** | The block keeps its shape — band distribution, counts — with names replaced by secret-derived pseudonyms. The control is visible rather than hidden behind a 403 |
| Dossiers, registries, co-offender graph, officer roster, copilot | **403** | There is no partial version of an individual's file worth rendering |
| `/sync`, `/settings`, `/audit-log*`, `/retention/*`, `/subject-report/ `, `/contests` | **Supervisor** | Administrative mutation and access review |

Enforcement is a decorator applied at the route, plus one property test
(`tests/test_api.py::test_no_offender_name_leaks_to_anonymous_callers`) that sweeps
every route without credentials and fails if any real registry name appears in any
response body. A per-route assertion only covers the routes someone remembered to
list; the sweep keeps holding as routes are added.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
**Every person-level access is audited** — actor, role, the *subject's* identifier,
the stated reason, IP, result — to stdout as JSON and to `audit.jsonl`. Reading the
audit log is itself audited. Callers may supply `X-Access-Reason`; accesses without
one are recorded as `reason_given: false` so unjustified lookups are visible in
review rather than indistinguishable. `AUDIT_REQUIRE_REASON=1` makes it mandatory.

**Person names never reach the LLM providers.** The copilot injects real records
into prompts sent to Groq/NVIDIA — third-party services outside India. Names are
replaced with per-request aliases (`[PERSON_1]`) before egress and restored locally
in the answer, so the model keeps referential consistency and the provider never
sees a person. See `appsail/privacy.py` for the limits this does *not* cover.

Demo accounts are active only while `AUTH_ACCOUNTS` is unset. Passwords are stored
as scrypt hashes, `/auth/login` locks out after 8 failures in 5 minutes, and the
API does **not** serve credentials — the passwords below are documented here for
reviewers and nowhere else:

| Username | Password | Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `analyst` | `scrb-analyst` | analyst — aggregate only |
| `io` | `scrb-io` | investigator — adds case and dossier access |
| `sp` | `scrb-sp` | supervisor — full watchlist and audit log |
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
**Before any deployment holding real records**, set `AUTH_ACCOUNTS`
(`user:scrypt$salt$key:role`, generate with `python -c "import auth;
print(auth.hash_password('...'))"`), `AUTH_SECRET`, and `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` (a long
random value — without it the audit chain is unkeyed and someone with write access to
the log could recompute it). All three are declared empty in
`app-config.example.json`, and `predeploy_check.py` warns when `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` is
missing. `/auth/me` reports
`insecure_cleartext_accounts` if any configured account still stores a plain
password. The LLM copilot also needs real `GROQ_API_KEY` / `NVIDIA_API_KEY` values
in `app-config.json`; the placeholders ship disabled.

**Does the model still work?** Drift monitoring (`/api/models/drift`) answers a
narrower question than it appears to: it reports that the *inputs* moved, never that
the *answers* got worse. A model can hold `stable` on every feature while its
accuracy collapses — a change in charging practice, a new court, a shift in what gets
recorded.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
The only way to answer the real question is to write down what was predicted, wait,
and write down what happened. `POST /api/models/outcome` records a result;
`GET /api/models/performance` joins it to the score that preceded it and reports
realised Brier, per-band calibration, and a skill score against the only model that
needs no data — always predicting the base rate. Outcomes are matched to the most
recent prediction *at or before* the observation, never a later one, because scoring
a subject again after their case resolved and then measuring against that score
manufactures accuracy out of hindsight.

**No outcome from operational use has been recorded.** What the loop does contain is
a replay: `python replay_outcomes.py --apply` scores the held-out window through the
serving artifact and feeds its real recorded results back in. That is worth doing for
a reason beyond the demo — offline evaluation scores a model inside the training
script, while serving loads a joblib and scores a frame rebuilt elsewhere, and those
two paths can silently diverge. Comparing them catches training/serving skew:
measured, both models agree with their published ROC-AUC to +0.0000.

Every replayed entry carries `source="replay"`, `realised()` reports the breakdown by
source, and the models page says so above the numbers — so a replayed figure can
never be read as field performance.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
**Audit integrity.** Every entry carries its sequence number, the digest of the entry
before it, and its own digest, so an edit, reorder or deletion breaks every digest
that follows. `GET /api/audit-log/verify` (supervisor-only, and itself audited)
recomputes the chain and names the first line that disagrees. Set `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY`
and the digests are keyed, so someone with file access cannot recompute the chain;
without it the chain still catches corruption and careless edits, and says so.

**What this is not.** A chain cannot detect its own truncation — dropping the newest
lines leaves a shorter chain that verifies perfectly — so that is checked against the
writer's own entry count while the process lives, and against the forwarded stdout
copy across restarts. Nor does any of it defend against a compromised application
process, which can still write false entries. A real deployment must still forward
those lines to an append-only store outside the application's trust boundary.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
**Contestability.** `GET /api/subject-report/ ` assembles everything the system
holds and asserts about one person — every score with its date, each model's stated
limits, who accessed the record and why, and any challenge raised. `POST /api/contest`
records a challenge (grounds required); the register is consulted on the serving path,
so a contested score reaches the officer marked. Filing does not suppress the score:
adjudication is the deploying authority's decision, and GOVERNANCE.md lists it as the
open gap.

**Retention and erasure.** `GET /api/retention` publishes what personal data is held,
for how long, and why. `POST /api/retention/erase` removes a subject's scores and
recorded outcomes; `POST /api/retention/purge` drops anything past its schedule. Both
preview by default and require `{"apply": true}` to write. Erasure deliberately does
not touch the access log — that records who viewed a file, and a log the subject could
delete would let anyone who improperly viewed a record destroy the proof by filing in
their name. A retention pass runs on every container start when
`RETENTION_ENFORCE=1`, and logs the backlog even when it is unset — AppSail has no
scheduler, so a restart is the only recurring event this application can hook.
GOVERNANCE.md lists what that still leaves open.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › Access control and audit

chunks.text:
What this platform is for, what it must not be used for, and the limits it operates
under are stated in **GOVERNANCE.md** — and, more usefully, served
next to the numbers they qualify. Every model carries a card in the registry giving
its intended use, out-of-scope use, the threshold anything acts on, what to monitor,
its retrain cadence, owner and review date. The `/models` page renders them beside
the metrics, because governance in a separate document drifts from the system it
governs.

The machine-readable source is `MODEL_CARDS` / `GOVERNANCE` in
`appsail/ml/config.py`; a model published without a card
raises a warning in its own training report.

Three things are worth stating here too:

* **No output is evidence.** Risk scores, conviction outlooks and link predictions
 allocate attention. None may be presented to a court as such.
* **No output triggers an action.** Every threshold orders a queue for a person to
 work; none authorises an action against an individual.
* **Known gaps are listed, not omitted** — challenge adjudication, scheduled
 retention enforcement, recorded outcomes and DPIA sign-off are all absent, and
 GOVERNANCE.md says so. `DPIA.md` carries the assessment as far as the code allows
 and marks the rest `[AUTHORITY]` rather than inventing it.

the model learned from, and reported next to the trivial baseline it has to beat.
The full evidence — split dates, confusion matrices, calibration curves, feature
importances and the warnings each run raised — is served at `/models` and lives in
`appsail/artifacts/model_registry.json`.

> **Read this before quoting a number.** The corpus is CCTNS-schema-shaped
> *simulated* data with a documented data-generating process
> (`simulate_outcomes.py`). These scores show that the
> pipeline can recover a structure we deliberately injected — the right thing to
> verify before real records exist — and are **not** claims of field performance on
> live KSP data. The same pipeline runs unchanged on a real extract by pointing
> `ml/dataset.py` at it.

> **Several of these numbers went *down* in the 31-district rebuild, and that is the
> point.** The earlier corpus had 800 offenders carrying 5,000 cases, so 98% of the
> registry were repeat offenders and "will this person reoffend?" was nearly always
> yes — an easy question that flattered the score. The rebuilt corpus has 9,000
> offenders, 29% of whom appear exactly once, which is the shape of a real docket.

chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models

chunks.text:
The first credibility test this platform has to pass is not a model score. It is
whether a SCRB officer scrolling the district filter sees their own district.

The corpus previously ran on **ten** districts, and two of the ten were not
districts at all:

* **Mangaluru** is the headquarters of Dakshina Kannada and a separate police
 commissionerate. Listing it *beside* Dakshina Kannada double-counted the same
 territory.
* **Hubballi-Dharwad** is a commissionerate covering the twin cities. The revenue
 district is **Dharwad**.

`appsail/karnataka.py` is now the single source of truth,
and every consumer — the generator, the outcome simulator, the socio-economic
overlay — reads from it, so the geography cannot drift between them.

| | Before | Now |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Districts | 10 (2 of them not districts) | **31**, the real set incl. Vijayanagara |
| Police commissionerates | not modelled | **8**, kept separate from the district list |
| Police stations | 28 | **140**, real town/locality names |
| District case volume | `random.choice()` — uniform | **population-weighted** (2011 Census) |
| Cases | 5,000 | **18,000** |
| Offenders | 800 (98% repeat offenders) | **9,000** (29% appear exactly once) |
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 0. 🗺️ Administrative Geography — All 31 Karnataka Districts

chunks.text:
**Why the weighting matters.** Drawing districts uniformly gave Kodagu (5.5 lakh
people) the same annual caseload as Bengaluru Urban (96 lakh). Every per-capita
rate, district ranking and hotspot comparison computed on top of that was
meaningless. Case volume now tracks population at r > 0.9, and the largest
district carries 18.8× the smallest — matching the 17.4× population ratio.

**What is real vs. modelled**, stated per column rather than blurred:

* **Real (2011 Census / KSP structure):** district names and count, the 8
 commissionerates, population, urbanisation, literacy. Yadgir genuinely has the
 lowest literacy in Karnataka (51.8%) and Dakshina Kannada among the highest
 (88.6%).
* **Approximate:** district-HQ coordinates, accurate to roughly a kilometre. They
 anchor the incident scatter; they are not survey-grade boundaries and the
 platform never claims they are.
* **Derived estimates:** per-capita income, unemployment, police density, youth
 share and slum share, computed from the census series by documented formulas in
 `generate_socioeconomic.py`. Internally
 coherent and correctly ordered, but not measured figures.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 0. 🗺️ Administrative Geography — All 31 Karnataka Districts

chunks.text:
A guard test asserts each district's incident centroid is nearest **its own**
headquarters — the property that actually matters — rather than a fixed distance
threshold, because real geography defeats thresholds: Koppal and Hosapete
(Vijayanagara) are genuinely ~20 km apart.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 0. 🗺️ Administrative Geography — All 31 Karnataka Districts

chunks.text:
* Weekly incident counts up to 8 weeks ahead, state-wide, per district and per crime type.
* **Walk-forward backtested** across 6 expanding-window origins — the model is re-fitted
 at each origin and scored only on the weeks after it, the way a forecast would
 actually have been issued.
* Prediction intervals are built from **out-of-sample backtest residuals at each
 horizon step**, not from in-sample residuals, so the stated 80% is measurable —
 realised coverage is 77%.
* Reported honestly: it beats naive, seasonal-naive and drift, but **does not beat a
 4-week moving average**. At this weekly volume the series is close to
 noise-dominated, and the registry says so.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 1. 📈 Crime Volume Forecasting (RidgeCV + Fourier Seasonality)

chunks.text:
* `eps` and `min_samples` are **chosen by a 32-point sweep** scored on silhouette and
 noise fraction, not hard-coded. The full sweep is published so the choice is auditable.
* Cluster count and zone radius are constrained to what a command centre can staff:
 silhouette alone rewards both hundreds of four-incident micro-clusters *and* one
 district-sized blob, neither of which is a patrol plan.
* Incidents left unclustered are reported as genuinely dispersed rather than forced
 into an invented hotspot.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 2. 📍 Geospatial Hotspot Zones (Haversine DBSCAN, parameters selected)

chunks.text:
* Force-directed network across suspects, FIRs, officers, cyber identifiers and vehicles,
 with 1st/2nd-degree sub-graph extraction.
* **Adamic-Adar link prediction** surfaces emerging co-offender alliances.
* **Louvain community detection** runs on the *offender projection* of the graph and
 requires repeat co-offending, so a "syndicate" is a set of people who work together
 more than once — not a set of case nodes.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 3. 🕸️ Link Analysis, Syndicate Detection & Link Prediction

chunks.text:
* Predicts whether an offender is named in a **new case within 365 days** of an
 observation date. Training and test panels are observed a year apart so their
 outcome windows never overlap.
* Undated snapshot columns (`past_fir_count`, `risk_level`, `active_warrant`) are
 **excluded** — they may already count the offences being predicted. Prior counts are
 recomputed from dated case and arrest records. An ablation quantifies exactly what
 those columns would have added.
* The watchlist index is a **percentile rank** with the calibrated probability shown
 alongside, and never displays 0% or 100%.
* Reported honestly: the previous hand-weighted rubric, restricted to the same dated
 information, scores 0.708 — statistically indistinguishable from the learned model's
 0.709. Reading the undated snapshot columns lifts that same rubric to 0.772, which is
 exactly the inflation those columns were excluded to prevent.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 4. ⚖️ Recidivism Risk (supervised, calibrated)

chunks.text:
* Reads FIR free text and assigns a crime head, so uncategorised reports can be triaged.
* Hyper-parameters are grid-searched **inside the training window only**; the test
 window is touched once.
* A **leakage probe** flags any token that appears in only one class, and its findings
 are published rather than suppressed.
* Errors fall where a human clerk's would: Murder↔Homicide↔Assault, and the property
 trio. Cyber fraud separates cleanly (precision 1.00, recall 0.99) because its
 vocabulary genuinely differs.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 5. 📝 FIR Narrative Crime Classifier (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression)

chunks.text:
* **Trial outcome** predicts conviction vs acquittal for a named accused, split so no
 individual appears on both sides *and* the test half is later in time. Performance is
 broken out by age band and gender so a model that works overall but fails a subgroup
 cannot pass unnoticed.
* **Case progression** predicts a chargesheet within 180 days of registration — a
 time-boxed target using real chargesheet dates, replacing the undefined
 `status == 'Closed'` snapshot. Officer `closure_rate`, `cases_assigned` and
 `commendations` are **banned features**: they are aggregates of case outcomes and
 contained the label.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 6. ⚖️ Trial Outcome & Case Progression

chunks.text:
* **Models right-censoring instead of discarding it.** The binary case-progression
 model above must exclude every case registered in the last 180 days of the extract,
 because those cases have not had time to answer "chargesheet within 180 days?".
 Those are precisely the files sitting open on a desk today — it is structurally
 incapable of scoring the live docket. **1,314 cases** on this corpus, and **56.5% of
 the test window**, are censored rows that it either drops or mislabels.
* **Discrete-time survival via person-period expansion** — sklearn only, no new
 dependency. Each case becomes one row per 30-day interval it survived into; a
 classifier on those rows *is* an estimator of the discrete hazard `h(k | x)`, and
 chaining gives the survival curve `S(t | x)`.
* **One model answers every horizon.** The 60 / 90 / 180 / 360-day figures are read
 off the same curve rather than coming from four separate classifiers that could
 contradict each other.
* **Beaten against Kaplan-Meier**, the covariate-free curve — the only honest
 reference for a survival model. C-index 0.611 against a coin-flip floor of 0.500,
 and integrated Brier 0.209 against the baseline's 0.241. It has to win on *both*
 the ranking metric and the proper scoring rule, and it does.
* **Conditional on time already served.** Risk is quoted from today, not from
 registration, and is interpolated *within* the 30
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 6b. ⏳ Case Pendency — Survival Analysis on the Live Docket

chunks.text:
-day interval — otherwise a case
 open 35 days reads as certain to still be open at day 60 purely because both fall
 in the same grid cell.
* **It refuses to score 88% of the open docket.** Cases open longer than the model's
 360-day observation grid are reported as a counted structural backlog and are
 deliberately **not** given a probability: no comparable training case was still
 unresolved at that age, so a number there would be extrapolation dressed up as a
 measurement. Printing "97% risk" against a six-year-old file launders an
 administrative fact as a model output. The refusal is the feature.
* **Triage ranks on expected remaining days, not breach probability.** A case at day
 359 scores ~100% against its 360-day horizon simply because one day is left — true,
 but useless. Remaining time discriminates across the whole docket (167–338 days on
 this corpus) and surfaces newly-registered cases predicted to drag, while
 intervening still changes the outcome.
* Served at `/serverless/api/pendency` and rendered at `/pendency`.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🚀 Key Platform Features & ML Models › 6b. ⏳ Case Pendency — Survival Analysis on the Live Docket

chunks.text:
* **It reads the records instead of a summary.** `appsail/copilot_engine.py` gives the copilot
 retrieval tools over every table: a full case dossier (narrative, accused with priors and flags,
 victim, complainant, IO, arrests, chargesheet, court stage, stolen vehicles, cyber identifiers,
 CCTV, Dial-112, pendency score, similar-MO cases), a person profile (every case they are named in,

 (`appsail/copilot_knowledge.py`).
* **LLM tool-calling loop.** Groq `llama-3.3-70b-versatile` (NVIDIA fallback) decides which tools to
 call and chains them. Records the question names are resolved and pre-fetched first, so a typical
 answer costs one round trip.
* **Works with no API key.** The same entity resolution and tools drive a deterministic engine that
 composes the answer when no provider is configured or all of them fail.
* **Knows the platform as it is today.** `appsail/build_project_knowledge.py` indexes every
 Markdown document, backend module docstring, API route (with the role it requires) and web page
 into `appsail/artifacts/project_knowledge.json`. The copilot searches it, rebuilds it in memor

chunks.text:
y
 in a full checkout whenever a source is newer, and reads the running system directly for live
 routes and tables. **After changing docs, routes or pages, run
 `python appsail/build_project_knowledge.py` and commit the result** — CI fails otherwise.
* **Scope.** It searches only IntelHub's own role-gated, audited records — never the internet,

* **Conversation memory.** "this case", "he", "her" resolve to the record on screen or the subject of

* **Same safeguards as before, applied to more data.** Names in every tool result are aliased before

* **Siri-style voice UI.** A live waveform that follows your microphone level and each word Kavya

chunks.text:
Offline evaluation describes a model on the day it was trained. These describe it
afterwards — the gap that matters more, because a model quietly applied to a
population it never learned from keeps returning confident numbers.

* **Prediction logging.** Every score handed to a person is recorded — model,
 subject, value, time — to stdout and `predictions.jsonl` (rotated at 16 MB). This
 is the raw material for a feedback loop: without a record of what was predicted,
 "was it right?" cannot be asked.
* **Drift detection.** Each tabular model stores the distribution of its own inputs
 and outputs at training time, and `GET /serverless/api/models/drift` reports
 Population Stability Index per feature against it — the standard credit-risk
 measure. Below 0.10 stable, 0.10–0.25 moderate, above 0.25 significant. The
 endpoint lists **every** model including the ones it cannot monitor (the text
 classifier, the forecast, the clustering) and why, so that silence never reads as
 safety.
* **Versioned artifacts and rollback.** `save_artifact` used to overwrite in place,
 so a bad training run replaced the working model with no way back. Every save now
 keeps the previous five under `artifacts/versions/ /`, and
 `registry.rollback(name)` steps back through them.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 📉 Runtime model operations

chunks.text:
What this deliberately does **not** claim: drift shows the *inputs* moved, never
that the answers got worse. That needs outcomes, and nothing yet records what
actually happened to the people scored. It is listed as the largest open gap in
GOVERNANCE.md.

---
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 📉 Runtime model operations

chunks.text:
Case registry and pendency docket views export to **CSV** or a **printable briefing**
(the browser's own print dialogue, so "Save as PDF" is already there — no 300 KB PDF
library). Both carry a provenance header recording when the extract was pulled, the
filters that produced it, and that the corpus is simulated. An extract that arrives
in a meeting with no indication of where it came from is exactly the artefact the
model registry exists to prevent.

chunks.title: 3. deploy › 📤 Taking work out of the platform

chunks.text:
Karnataka Police work in Kannada. The UI carries an EN / ಕನ್ನಡ switch, a real Kannada
webface (`Noto Sans Kannada`, previously absent so Kannada text fell back to whatever
the OS had), and ` ` kept in sync with the choice — it was hardcoded to
`en`, which made screen readers announce Kannada with English phonemes.

**The dictionary is deliberately small.** It covers navigation and ordinary UI
chrome. Police terminology has conventions that general translation gets wrong, and
machine-translating legal vocabulary into a police tool and calling it localised
would be the same overclaim this codebase has spent its effort removing. A missing
key falls back to English rather than a placeholder, and `missingKeys()` reports
what is uncovered. Domain vocabulary needs a Kannada-speaking officer before any
real deployment.

chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🌐 Bilingual interface

chunks.text:
Models are trained **offline**, not at server boot. One command produces both the
fitted estimators and the evidence:

 

 

**Why the split matters.** Crime records are events on a timeline. A random
`train_test_split` lets a model learn from cases registered *after* the ones it is
scored on, which silently inflates every metric. Every supervised model here is split
on time instead.

**Artifacts vs evidence.** `*.joblib` files are a boot-time speed optimisation and are
refused if the runtime's scikit-learn differs from the training build — in which case
the app retrains in-process from the same code, so the two paths cannot disagree.
`model_registry.json` is plain, portable JSON, is committed, and is what the UI
renders; it is never recomputed at request time.
chunks.title: 3. deploy › 🔬 Training & Evaluation Pipeline

chunks.text:
Every model is scored on a held-out window **later in time** than everything it
learned from, and printed next to the trivial rule it has to beat. A model that
cannot beat its baseline is not quietly dropped — it ships with the finding attached.

| Model | Result | Baseline it had to beat |
|---|---|---|
| FIR narrative classifier | accuracy **0.808** | 0.103 majority class — the clearest win in the set |
| Recidivism risk | ROC-AUC **0.709** | 0.500 coin flip; in line with COMPAS at 0.68–0.71 |
| Case pendency (survival) | IBS **0.209**, C-index 0.611 | 0.241 Kaplan–Meier with no covariates |
| Conviction outcome | ROC-AUC **0.675** | 0.500 coin flip |
| Case progression | ROC-AUC **0.646** | 0.500 coin flip |
| Hotspot clustering | silhouette **0.638**, 60 zones | unsupervised; 21.7% left as noise rather than forced into a cluster |
| Weekly crime forecast | MASE **0.640** | 0.911 naive — **but see below** |

**Two findings we publish rather than bury.**

*The forecast is not as good as its headline.* MASE 0.640 beats the naive forecast,
but a paired bootstrap against a four-week moving average puts the 95% confidence
interval on the difference across zero. The series carries little forecastable signal
beyond its local level, and the registry says so in those words. A registry that never
warns is a registry nobody reads.

chunks.text:
*We rejected a baseline that beat our own model.* A legacy-style scoring rubric scored
0.772 against our recidivism model's 0.709 — and we did not ship it. It reads
current-state columns that already reflect the outcome being predicted. Strip those
and the same rubric drops to 0.708. 0.709 is the honest number.

**Why this matters operationally.** Every one of these scores orders a queue — which
case to work next, which docket is about to breach its deadline, where to put a
patrol. None of them authorises an action against a named person, and the copilot
refuses in code when asked to.

The full registry — split dates, calibration curves, confusion matrices, per-horizon
metrics and the six warnings the training run raised — is committed at

chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document

chunks.text:
The **State Crime Records Bureau (SCRB), Karnataka State Police**, manages extensive historical crime data capturing registered First Information Reports (FIRs), accused individuals, victim profiles, court trial statuses, stolen vehicles, cyber crime complaints, and officer registries across Karnataka's districts. 

However, traditional law enforcement operations face four critical challenges:
1. **Siloed Data Registries**: Information is fragmented across disparate spreadsheets and manual reporting tools.
2. **Lack of Automated Predictive Analytics**: Inability to forecast weekly incident spikes or dynamically detect spatial crime clusters.
3. **Reactive Patrol Allocation**: Police patrols are dispatched reactively rather than proactively to high-risk zones.
4. **Opaque Co-Offender Networks**: Difficulty in tracing multi-layer connections between habitual offenders (Rowdy-Sheeters), cyber fraud rings, and stolen vehicle networks.

**KSP IntelHub** solves this by unifying 26 relational database tables across all 31 Karnataka districts into a single real-time intelligence core featuring machine learning predictive engines, 3D relational link prediction, and an interactive multilingual AI voice console.

---
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Problem Statement Addressed

chunks.text:
0. **🗺️ Correct Administrative Geography — All 31 Karnataka Districts**
 * The first credibility test is not a model score; it is whether a SCRB officer sees their own district in the filter. The corpus previously carried **ten** districts, two of which were not districts: **Mangaluru** is the HQ of Dakshina Kannada and a commissionerate, and **Hubballi-Dharwad** is a commissionerate whose revenue district is **Dharwad**.
 * Now **31 districts** (including Vijayanagara, carved from Ballari in 2021), **8 police commissionerates** kept structurally separate from the district list, and **140 police stations** under real town and locality names — all from one authoritative module, `appsail/karnataka.py`, that the generator, outcome simulator and socio-economic overlay all read from so the geography cannot drift between them.
 * **Case volume is population-weighted (2011 Census).** Uniform sampling had given Kodagu (5.5 lakh) the same caseload as Bengaluru Urban (96 lakh), which makes every per-capita rate and district ranking meaningless. Volume now tracks population at r > 0.9, with an 18.8× spread matching the 17.4× population ratio.
 * Corpus rebuilt to **18,000 cases and 9,000 offenders**. The old 800-offender registry meant 98% of people in it were repeat offenders and "will they reoffend?" was nearly always yes; **29% now appear exactly once**, which is the shape of a real do
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
cket.
 * **What is real vs. modelled is stated per column**: census figures for population, urbanisation and literacy (Yadgir genuinely lowest in Karnataka at 51.8%); approximate HQ coordinates for the incident scatter; and clearly-labelled derived estimates for income, unemployment, police density, youth and slum share.
 * A guard test asserts each district's incident centroid is nearest **its own** headquarters rather than using a distance threshold — real geography defeats thresholds, since Koppal and Hosapete are genuinely ~20 km apart.

1. **🕸️ 3D Holographic Link Analysis & Adamic-Adar Link Prediction**
 * Force-directed 3D/2D network topology visualizer mapping relationships between suspects, FIR cases, investigating officers, cyber identifiers (IP/IMEI), and stolen vehicles.
 * **Targeted Sub-Graph Extraction**: Restricts searches to immediate 1st/2nd degree relational networks, eliminating cluttered node blobs.
 * **Adamic-Adar Co-Offender Link Prediction**: Calculates structural network similarity to predict hidden alliances and emerging criminal partnerships.
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
2. **📈 Predictive Crime Forecasting (RidgeCV + Fourier Seasonality)**
 * Forecasts statewide and district-level weekly incident volumes up to 8 weeks ahead, with prediction intervals built from out-of-sample backtest residuals at each horizon step (realised coverage 77% against a nominal 80%).
 * **Walk-forward backtested** over 6 expanding-window origins: MASE 0.640, beating naive (0.911), seasonal-naive (0.686) and drift (0.927).
 * Reported honestly: it **ties a 4-week moving average** (0.765). At this weekly volume the series is close to noise-dominated, and the model registry states that rather than hiding it.

3. **📍 Geospatial Density & Patrol Optimization (KDE + DBSCAN)**
 * **Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)** calculates continuous spatial crime density.
 * **Haversine DBSCAN Clustering** groups incidents into bounded high-risk zones. `eps` and `min_samples` are **selected by a 32-point sweep** scored on silhouette and noise fraction — not hard-coded — and the full sweep is published for audit.
 * Selected configuration across 31 districts: 60 zones, silhouette 0.638, Davies-Bouldin 0.362, 6.3 km median radius — every zone small enough to actually dispatch a unit to.
 * Recommends patrol plans from cluster risk metrics.
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
4. **⚖️ Supervised Recidivism Risk (calibrated, ROC-AUC 0.709)**
 * Predicts whether an offender is **named in a new case within 365 days** of an observation date — a real, dated target rather than a hand-weighted rubric.
 * Training and test panels are observed a year apart so their outcome windows never overlap. Undated snapshot columns (`past_fir_count`, `risk_level`, `active_warrant`) are **excluded** because they may already count the offences being predicted; prior counts are recomputed from dated case and arrest records, and an ablation quantifies what those columns would have added.
 * The watchlist index is a **percentile rank** with the calibrated probability shown alongside (Brier 0.201), banded `Extreme` / `High` / `Elevated` / `Moderate`, and never displays a 0% or 100% certainty about a person.
 * Reported honestly: the previous rubric, restricted to the same dated information, scores 0.708 — indistinguishable from the learned model's 0.709. Letting that same rubric read the undated snapshot columns lifts it to 0.772, which is precisely the inflation those columns were excluded to prevent.
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
4b. **⚖️ Trial Outcome & Case Progression**
 * **Trial outcome** (ROC-AUC 0.674) flags evidentially weak prosecutions early. Split so no individual appears on both sides *and* the test half is later in time; performance is broken out by age band and gender.
 * **Case progression** (ROC-AUC 0.646) predicts a chargesheet within 180 days of registration — a time-boxed target using real chargesheet dates. Officer `closure_rate`, `cases_assigned` and `commendations` are **banned features**: they are aggregates of case outcomes and contained the label.
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
4c. **⏳ Case Pendency — Survival Analysis on the Live Docket**
 * **Discrete-time survival model** (person-period expansion, scikit-learn only) predicting *days from FIR registration to chargesheet*, with right-censoring modelled rather than discarded.
 * **This is the model that can score cases open today.** The binary case-progression model must exclude every case registered in the last 180 days, because they have not had time to answer "chargesheet within 180 days?" — precisely the files on an IO's desk right now. **56.5%** of the test window is censored; the survival model uses all of it.
 * **C-index 0.611** against a coin-flip floor of 0.500, and **integrated Brier 0.209** against the **Kaplan-Meier baseline's 0.241** — it has to beat the covariate-free curve on both the ranking metric and the proper scoring rule, and it does.
 * **One model, every horizon.** The 60 / 90 / 180 / 360-day SLA figures are read off a single survival curve instead of four classifiers that could contradict each other. Risk is conditional on time already served and interpolated *within* the 30-day interval, so a case open 35 days is not quoted as certain to still be open at day 60.
 * **It refuses to score 88% of the open docket.** Cases open beyond the model's 360-day observation grid are reported as a counted structural backlog and given **no probability at all** — no comparable training case
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
was still unresolved at that age, so a number there would be extrapolation dressed as a measurement. Printing "97% risk" against a six-year-old file launders an administrative fact as a model output. The refusal is a designed feature, shown on screen.
 * **Triage ranks on expected remaining days, not breach probability.** A case at day 359 scores ~100% against its 360-day horizon simply because one day is left. Remaining time discriminates across the whole docket and surfaces newly-registered cases predicted to drag — while intervening still changes the outcome.
 * Delivered as `/serverless/api/pendency` and the `/pendency` command view, with 26 dedicated guard tests.
chunks.title: 📋 KSP IntelHub — Solution Submission Document › 1. 📌 Prototype Brief › Key Features and Functionalities

chunks.text:
5. **📝 Explainable FIR Narrative Classifier (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression)**
 * Classifies uncategorised FIR narratives into 10 crime heads. **Accuracy 0.808, macro-F1 0.808** on a temporally held-out window, against a majority-class baseline of 0.103.
 * Hyper-parameters are grid-searched **inside the training window only**; the test window is touched once. Linear SVM (0.814) and Complement Naive Bayes (0.796) are reported as alternatives considered.
 * A **leakage probe** flags any token appearing in only one class, and publishes its findings rather than suppressing them.
 * Errors land where a human clerk's would — Murder↔Homicide↔Assault, and the property trio — while cyber fraud separates cleanly (precision 1.00, recall 0.99). Per-class precision/recall and the full confusion matrix are on the `/models` page.

6. **🤖 Multilingual AI Voice & Text Agent Console**
 * Voice & text HUD query console executing dynamic search queries across all 26 relational tables in English and Kannada.
 * Automatically executes smart contextual client-side routing (e.g., navigating to `/network?q=Kartik+Bhartiya` or `/intel?tab=courts&q=xyz`).

7. **🖥️ Native Command Center Full Screen Viewport**
 * One-click full screen toggle triggering native browser fullscreen mode and using CSS `:fullscreen` rules to hide navigation bars for command center displays.

chunks.text:
| Principle | What we do | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Temporal validation** | Every supervised model is split on time; the test window is strictly later than everything it learned from | Crime records are events on a timeline. A random split lets a model learn from cases registered *after* the ones it is scored on, which inflates every metric |
| **Baselines always** | Each score is reported next to majority-class / base-rate / naive / seasonal-naive references | 82% means nothing until you know the majority class scores 9.6% |
| **Leakage controls** | Banned-feature list, undated snapshot columns excluded, leakage probe on text, ablations that quantify what a leaky feature would have added | Three leaky features were found and removed during this work |
| **Calibration** | Probabilistic models scored with Brier and reliability bins, not just ranking | "72% likely to reoffend" is a claim about frequency; a miscalibrated score is actively misleading in policing |
| **Operational metrics** | Lift tables ("the top 20% of the watchlist contains 33% of reoffenders"), patrollable zone radius | AUC is abstract; a station needs to know what working the top slice buys |
| **Fairness slices** | Trial-outcome performance broken out by age band and gender | A model can look fine overall and fail a subgroup |
| **Publish the failures** | Warnings, baselines a model did not beat, and p

chunks.text:
robes that fired are rendered on the page, not suppressed | A registry that never warns is a registry nobody reads |
| **Reproducibility** | Seeded runs, git commit + library versions stamped into every report, 289 guard tests (`python -m pytest tests -q`) | The numbers must be re-derivable, not asserted |

**Honest limitations, stated up front.** The corpus is CCTNS-schema-shaped *simulated*
data with a documented data-generating process (`appsail/simulate_outcomes.py`). These
scores demonstrate that the pipeline recovers a structure we deliberately injected —
which validates the features, splits and evaluation before real records exist — and are
**not** claims of field performance. `appsail/ml/dataset.py` is the single adapter
layer: pointing it at a real KSP extract runs the identical pipeline with no model,
metric or endpoint changes.
