---------------
Every factual question put to the agent fell through to "I could not reach my
reasoning core" — "how many cases are there", "which district has the most crime",
"what is the conviction rate". All of it sits in `data_cache`; none of it needed a
language model. The copilot was advertising itself on every page and then declining
to answer the easiest questions in the product.

Two rules this module holds to
------------------------------
**Every number is computed, never asserted.** Each answer carries a `grounding` block
naming the figures it used and where they came from, so a reply can be checked rather
than believed. A handler that cannot compute its answer returns None and the caller
falls through — a wrong number stated confidently is worse than no answer.

**It refuses what the platform refuses.** GOVERNANCE.md says this system does not
infer guilt and that no output authorises an action against an individual. The
copilot is the surface most likely to be asked to do both, in exactly those words, and
it used to respond to "is SUS-1001 guilty" by quietly opening the dossier. A refusal
that explains itself is part of the control, not a limitation of it.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/agent_answers.py

chunks.text:
List-of-people questions route to the gated registry views rather than printing names
into a chat transcript. The route already requires `investigator`, so this is not
about access — a transcript is simply the wrong place for a watchlist.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/agent_answers.py

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub — advanced analytics & ML layer.

Pure, self-contained functions that take the loaded dataframes / knowledge graph and
return JSON-serialisable intelligence. Kept out of main.py so the model code is
independently testable and the request layer stays thin. Everything degrades gracefully:
any model that can't fit (missing columns, too little data) returns an empty result
instead of raising, so a partial dataset never takes the API down.

What lives here, and what does not
----------------------------------
This module holds the **graph-derived** intelligence — the parts that depend on the
NetworkX knowledge graph built at load time rather than on a fitted model:

* Adamic-Adar link prediction over the co-offender network
* Louvain community detection (syndicates), on the offender projection
* Socio-economic correlation
* Case↔suspect matching and per-suspect correlation reports

Everything supervised — forecasting, hotspot clustering, the narrative classifier,
recidivism, conviction, case progression, pendency — lives in `ml/tasks/` and is
trained offline with temporal validation. Seven functions here reimplemented those
models and were deleted: they had become a closed cluster that nothing reachable
called, and an untested second implementation alongside a tested one is how the two
diverge and someone edits the wrong copy.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/analytics.py

chunks.text:
Access audit trail for person-level data.

Why this exists
---------------
Before this module the platform had no audit trail of any kind. A repo-wide search
for `audit` returned exactly one hit — a subtitle string in the UI. That means a
supervisor could pull the full recidivism watchlist for every district in Karnataka
and there would be no evidence, anywhere, that it had happened.

For a police record system that is disqualifying on its own, and it is disqualifying
independently of whether the access control works. Access control decides who *may*
look; the audit trail is what makes anyone accountable for having looked. A system
that gates perfectly and logs nothing still cannot answer the only question that
matters after a leak: who read this person's file?

What is recorded
----------------
One JSON object per access to person-level data:
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/audit.py

chunks.text:
ts          UTC timestamp, ISO-8601
    actor       authenticated username, or null
    role        the role the request was served at
    route       the Flask rule that matched
    action      what was done, e.g. "read_offender_dossier"
    subject     type + identifier of the *person or case* accessed — not just the
                endpoint. "GET /api/suspect" is useless six months later;
                "read_offender_dossier SUS-1042" is evidence.
    reason      the stated purpose, if the caller supplied one
    ip          best-effort client address
    result      ok | denied | error
    status      HTTP status returned

Where it goes
-------------
Two sinks, deliberately:

* **stdout**, prefixed `AUDIT `, as a single JSON line. AppSail's filesystem is
  ephemeral, so the container log is the only sink that survives a restart today.
* **a local JSONL file**, for development and for deployments with a real disk.

Neither is tamper-evident, and this module does not pretend otherwise — see
`INTEGRITY_NOTE`. A production deployment must ship these lines to an append-only
store outside the application's own trust boundary. What is fixed here is the
absence of a record; hardening where that record lives is a deployment decision.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/audit.py

chunks.text:
Reason-for-access
-----------------
Real police record systems require an officer to state why they are opening a
file, because the log is only useful if it distinguishes legitimate case work from
browsing. Callers may supply `X-Access-Reason` (or `?reason=`). It is recorded, and
`reason_given: false` is recorded when it is absent, so unjustified access is
visible in review rather than indistinguishable. Setting `AUDIT_REQUIRE_REASON=1`
turns that from an observation into a hard requirement.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/audit.py

chunks.text:
Role-based access control for person-level data.

Design intent
-------------
Aggregate intelligence and person-level intelligence are not the same thing and
must not carry the same access rules. "Kalaburagi has a 34% chargesheet rate" is a
management statistic. "These 40 named people are ranked by how likely we think
they are to offend again" is a dossier about individuals, and it is the single
most sensitive artefact this platform produces.

So the gate is placed there rather than across the whole application:

* **Statistical / aggregate surfaces stay open.** District funnels, forecasts,
  hotspot zones, the model registry — none of it identifies anyone.
* **Person-level surfaces are redacted, not refused.** An unauthenticated caller
  still gets the watchlist *shape* — how many people, the band distribution, the
  method — with names replaced by stable pseudonyms and calibrated probabilities
  withheld. Authorised callers get the full record.

Redaction rather than a 403 is deliberate. A hard refusal hides that the control
exists; a redacted response demonstrates it working, and lets an evaluator see
both states side by side without credentials.

Roles are ordered. A caller always has at least `analyst`, so the platform is
usable without signing in and nothing silently breaks.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/auth.py

chunks.text:
Secrets
-------
`AUTH_SECRET` signs tokens; absent, a random per-process secret is generated, so
tokens simply do not survive a restart. That is the safe default — it is never a
hardcoded fallback secret, which would be worse than none.

`AUTH_ACCOUNTS` holds credentials as `user:password:role,user:password:role`.
Absent, the demo accounts below are enabled and the API advertises that it is
running in demo mode. **Set AUTH_ACCOUNTS before any real deployment.**
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/auth.py

chunks.text:
Build the copilot's knowledge of the platform from the repository itself.

Why this exists
---------------
`copilot_knowledge.TOPICS` is hand-written. It was accurate the day it was written
and starts drifting the first time someone adds a page, a route or a model without
remembering to update it — which is every time. The copilot then describes a
platform that no longer exists, confidently.

This script reads what the repository actually contains and writes it to
`artifacts/project_knowledge.json`:

* every Markdown document at the repo root, split by heading;
* the module docstring of every backend module (`appsail/*.py`, `appsail/ml/**`);
* every API route in `main.py` — path, methods, the role it requires, its docstring;
* every page of the web client — its URL and the headings and copy it shows.

The artifact is committed because AppSail deploys `appsail/` alone, so the docs and
the web client are not on disk in production. In a full checkout the copilot
rebuilds it in memory whenever a source file is newer than the artifact, and CI runs
`python build_project_knowledge.py --check`, which fails when the committed copy is
stale. Change the project, run this once, commit — and the copilot knows.

Usage:
    python build_project_knowledge.py          # rebuild the artifact
    python build_project_knowledge.py --check  # exit 1 if it is out of date
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/build_project_knowledge.py

chunks.text:
Contestability: a person's route to challenge what the system says about them.

Why this exists
---------------
The governance statement claims these models "order a queue for a person to work" and
that no output authorises an action against an individual. Both are true, and both
are weaker than they sound while a person has no way to find out they are on a
watchlist, no way to see why, and no way to object. Automated assessment without a
route to challenge it is the failure mode every framework for this — the DPDP Act's
grievance redressal duty included — exists to prevent.

Three things are needed and all three are here:

1. **Disclosure.** `subject_report` assembles everything the system holds and asserts
   about one person: every score with its date, the model's own stated limits, who
   accessed the record and why. A person cannot contest an assessment they cannot see.
2. **A record of the challenge.** `raise_contest` writes it down, against a specific
   subject and model, with the grounds stated.
3. **Consequence.** `is_contested` is checked at serving time, so a contested score
   travels marked wherever it is displayed. A challenge that changed nothing about
   what the officer sees would be a complaints box, not a control.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/contest.py

chunks.text:
What this deliberately does not do
----------------------------------
It does not adjudicate. Nothing here decides whether a challenge is well-founded, and
nothing automatically suppresses a score — that is a decision for the deploying
authority, not for this module to make silently. What it guarantees is that the
challenge is recorded, disclosed alongside the assessment, and visible to whoever
acts on it.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/contest.py

chunks.text:
The copilot's reasoning core: retrieval tools over the live corpus, an LLM
tool-calling loop, and a deterministic engine that answers when no model is reachable.

Why this exists
---------------
The copilot used to see the corpus through one twenty-line aggregate briefing plus a
substring search that returned six rows per table. Asked about a specific FIR it knew
the crime type and status and nothing else; asked about a person it knew a name and a
risk band; asked a follow-up ("who else was in that case?") it had nothing to look at.
It answered fluently anyway, which is worse than not answering.

This module gives it the same view of a record an investigator has:
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/copilot_engine.py

chunks.text:
* **Tools** that read the full record — a case with its narrative, accused, victim,
  complainant, IO, arrests, chargesheet, court stage, linked vehicles, cyber
  identifiers, CCTV and Dial-112 calls; a person with every case they are named in,
  co-offenders, syndicates, risk drivers and court outcomes; officers; registries;
  filtered counts and breakdowns; paths through the link graph; every ML output; and
  the platform's own documentation (`copilot_knowledge`).
* **An LLM loop** (OpenAI-compatible tool calling) that decides which tools to call,
  reads the results, and answers. Entities the question names are resolved and
  pre-fetched before the first call, so the common case costs one round trip.
* **A deterministic engine** that resolves the same entities and composes an answer
  from the same tools when no provider is configured or all of them fail. The demo
  must not depend on a third-party API being up.

Rules it holds to
-----------------
* Every tool result sent to a provider has person names replaced with request-scoped
  aliases (`privacy.mask`) and contact numbers dropped; answers are restored locally.
* Tools return what is recorded and say what is missing. They never fill a gap.
* Ranked lists of people (watchlists) are returned as identifiers and scores, never
  names — the platform's stated position (agent_answers._watchlist).
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/copilot_engine.py

chunks.text:
What the copilot knows about the platform itself.

Two layers:

* **Curated topics** (`TOPICS`) — a short, hand-checked summary of what the platform
  is, its pages, data, models, governance and policing vocabulary. Fast and always
  available, but it only changes when someone edits it.
* **The generated index** — `artifacts/project_knowledge.json`, built from the
  repository by `build_project_knowledge.py`: every Markdown document by heading,
  every backend module docstring, every API route with its required role, every
  web page with its headings and copy. In a full checkout it is rebuilt in memory
  whenever a source file is newer than the artifact, so the copilot describes the
  project as it is today, not as it was when this file was last edited.

`search()` ranks both layers together (BM25 over the index, with curated topics
boosted), and `describe_live()` reads the running system — routes from Flask's URL
map, tables from the loaded corpus — which cannot go stale at all.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/copilot_knowledge.py

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub — CCTNS-style synthetic data generator.

Augments the existing FIR table and produces an interconnected web of records
(criminals, officers, stolen vehicles, CCTV, complaints, cybercrime trails,
missing persons, court cases) so the knowledge graph and AI can correlate
across entities the way a real Crime & Criminal Tracking system does.

Deterministic (seeded) so results are reproducible. Run:  python generate_data.py
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_data.py

chunks.text:
Realistic FIR narrative corpus generator.

Why this file replaces `generate_narratives.py`
-----------------------------------------------
The previous generator wrote one lexically distinct template block per crime type
— its own docstring said the blocks were kept distinct "so TF-IDF can separate the
classes cleanly". That makes the downstream classifier circular: the label is
recoverable from the template fingerprint, so a reported ">90% accuracy" measures
the generator, not the model. It also embedded the legal section ("Booked under
IPC Sec 384"), which names the offence outright.

This generator builds a corpus a text classifier can be honestly evaluated on:
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_fir_narratives.py

chunks.text:
* **A shared police register.** Every narrative is assembled from the same
  scaffold and the same body of station vocabulary (mahazar, panchanama, seizure
  memo, IO, complainant, hobli) regardless of offence. Class-neutral words
  dominate the token count, as they do in real FIRs.
* **Overlapping, probabilistic vocabulary.** Distinctive phrasing is drawn with
  probability, not certainty, and confusable offences share a common pool. A
  narrative therefore *leans* toward its class rather than announcing it.
* **Genuinely confusable families.** Murder / Homicide / Assault sit in one pool
  and Chain Snatching / Vehicle Theft / House Break-in in another, because those
  heads genuinely overlap in the field. The resulting confusion matrix is a real
  criminological finding rather than an artefact to hide.
* **Terse and degraded reports.** ~16% of entries are two-line stubs and a small
  share carry transcription noise, mirroring how uneven station-level data entry
  actually is. These are the hard cases that keep the score honest.
* **No label giveaways.** Section numbers, crime-head names and the structured
  [METADATA:] tag are excluded from the narrative text.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_fir_narratives.py

chunks.text:
The structured metadata tag is still appended to CaseMaster.BriefFacts, because
the loader parses severity/weapon/vehicle/target from it — but it is written
*after* the narrative and stripped before any text model sees it.

Deterministic (seeded). Run:  python generate_fir_narratives.py
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_fir_narratives.py

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub — rich FIR narrative generator.

The original case_reports.csv narratives were short, near-identical templates that
share generic vocabulary across crime types, which capped the narrative classifier at
~69% and made free-text classification unreliable. This regenerates report_text for
every FIR with varied, crime-distinctive, evidence-rich language grounded in each
case's own attributes (station, weapon, target, vehicle, time, victim, casualties).

Keyed by the SAME case_id set as firs.csv, so nothing downstream (graph, links) changes
— only the narrative text gets richer. Deterministic (seeded). Run:

    python generate_narratives.py
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_narratives.py

chunks.text:
Generate a valid Postgres schema for the corpus.

Why this was rewritten
----------------------
The previous version guessed primary keys with a substring heuristic: any column
whose name contained "masterid" became `PRIMARY KEY`. Three tables therefore
declared several — `Accused` two, `Victim` two, `ArrestSurrender` three — which
Postgres rejects outright. The file it produced had never been executed, and
nothing in the codebase read it, so the error sat there undetected.

It also inferred types from `nrows=10`, so a column that is integer in its first
ten rows and null afterwards came out `BIGINT` and would fail on load.

What this does instead
----------------------
Keys are **declared**, not guessed. A schema is a set of assertions about the
data — that a case has one row, that an accused row points at a real case — and
those assertions have to be written down by someone who knows the domain, not
pattern-matched off column names.

Types are inferred from the whole file. Foreign keys and the indexes the query
paths actually need are emitted, because the point of moving off CSVs is to stop
doing full scans, and an unindexed table gives you the scans back with more
ceremony.

Run:  python generate_schema.py [--check]
      --check validates the existing schema.sql instead of rewriting it.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_schema.py

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub — district socio-economic indicators for all 31 Karnataka districts.

Supplies the one Challenge-02 capability the FIR tables cannot express on their
own: socio-economic crime correlation — the "why" behind the "where".

**What is real and what is modelled.** This distinction is published rather than
blurred, because a correlation is only as trustworthy as the weakest series in it:

* `population_lakh`, `urbanization`, `literacy` — **2011 Census figures.** Real,
  externally checkable numbers. Yadgir really does have the lowest literacy in
  Karnataka (51.8%) and Dakshina Kannada among the highest (88.6%).
* `per_capita_income_k`, `unemployment`, `police_per_100k`, `youth_pct`,
  `slum_pct` — **deterministic estimates derived from the census series above**
  by the documented formulas below. They are internally coherent and ordered
  correctly across districts, but they are not measured figures and must not be
  quoted as such. Swapping in a real DES/NCRB extract means replacing this file
  and nothing else.

Deterministic — no RNG. Run:  python generate_socioeconomic.py
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/generate_socioeconomic.py

chunks.text:
Check that the identifiers a model names actually exist.

The problem
-----------
The copilot's freeform `reply` was passed to the client verbatim. Nothing verified
it, and the system prompt actively pushed the other way — *"ASSERTIVE REASONING:
You may reason, infer, rank, and recommend. Act confidently"* — over a 1024-token
channel with no output validation. The reply was then **spoken aloud** by the
browser, which makes an invented statement sound more authoritative, not less.

In a policing context the specific danger is narrow and serious: a fluent sentence
naming a case or a person that does not exist, or attributing an offence to the
wrong identifier. That is not a hallucination an operator can spot, because it
looks exactly like the true ones.

What this does, and does not do
-------------------------------
It extracts every identifier-shaped token from a reply — case numbers, offender
ids, officer KGIDs — and checks each against the loaded corpus. Unknown ones are
returned so the caller can mark the answer as unverified.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/grounding.py

chunks.text:
This grounds *references*, not *claims*. "SUS-1042 has 9 prior cases" is verified
only insofar as SUS-1042 exists; the count is not checked. Verifying arbitrary
natural-language claims against a relational corpus is a much larger problem, and
pretending this solves it would be its own form of overclaiming. What it does
reliably catch is the invented identifier, which is the failure that turns a
plausible answer into a wrong one about a real person.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/grounding.py

chunks.text:
Canonical Karnataka geography — the single source of truth for districts.

Why this module exists
----------------------
The corpus previously ran on **ten** districts, and two of the ten were not
districts at all:

* **Mangaluru** is not a district. It is the headquarters of Dakshina Kannada,
  and separately a police commissionerate. Listing it alongside Dakshina Kannada
  double-counted the same territory.
* **Hubballi-Dharwad** is a police commissionerate covering the twin cities. The
  revenue district is **Dharwad**.

Karnataka has **31 districts**. Any SCRB officer reading a district filter that
stops at ten — and that contains a city where a district should be — knows the
data is invented before they look at a single model. Getting the administrative
geography right is not cosmetic; it is the first credibility test the platform
has to pass.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/karnataka.py

chunks.text:
What is authoritative here vs. approximate
------------------------------------------
* **District names and count** — authoritative. All 31, including Vijayanagara,
  carved out of Ballari in 2021.
* **Police commissionerates** — authoritative. Karnataka has 8; they are a
  separate command structure from the revenue districts and are flagged rather
  than mixed into the district list.
* **Headquarters coordinates** — approximate district-HQ positions, accurate to
  roughly a kilometre. They anchor the synthetic incident scatter; they are not
  survey-grade boundaries, and the platform never claims they are.
* **Population** — 2011 Census figures in lakhs, with Ballari/Vijayanagara split
  apportioned. Used to weight synthetic case volume so that Bengaluru Urban does
  not generate the same caseload as Kodagu. Real 2026 figures would differ; the
  point is the *relative* weighting, which is what makes per-capita rates and
  district comparisons meaningful at all.
* **Urban share** — 2011 Census urban population percentage, used for the
  socio-economic overlay.
* **Police station names** — real town and locality names within each district.
  The station roster is representative, not the complete KSP establishment list.

Every consumer — the generator, the outcome simulator, the socio-economic
overlay — reads from here, so the geography cannot drift between them.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/karnataka.py

chunks.text:
Load the CSV corpus into a real relational database.

Why this exists
---------------
The platform's whole claim about portability rests on one sentence: `ml/dataset.py`
is the only module that knows the physical schema, so pointing it at a different
source runs the identical pipeline. That claim was never tested. Every path still
ended at `pd.read_csv`.

This is the smallest thing that actually tests it. It builds a database from the
generated schema, loads the CSVs into it, and `ml.dataset.load_canonical(source=...)`
can then read from there instead — same canonical frames, same models, same metrics.

SQLite, not Postgres, on purpose: it needs no server, so the migration path can be
exercised in CI and on a laptop. The DDL in `schema.sql` is Postgres-flavoured and
SQLite accepts it, which is convenient rather than accidental — the types were chosen
to be portable. A Postgres deployment runs the same file.

What this does NOT do
---------------------
It does not make the application read from the database. `main.py` still loads the
CSV corpus into memory at boot, and the 512 MB ceiling and the missing write path are
unchanged. This proves the boundary holds and gives the migration something concrete
to build on; it is a foundation, not the finished job.

Run:  python load_to_db.py [--db corpus.db] [--verify]
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/load_to_db.py

chunks.text:
Structured logging, request correlation, and honest error responses.

What this replaces
------------------
The application had no `logging` import at all. Forty-seven `print()` calls went to
gunicorn's stdout with no timestamp, no level, no request correlation and no way to
filter. There was also no error handler, so an unhandled exception returned
Werkzeug's HTML page — from an API whose frontend parses JSON everywhere, which
turns a 500 into a confusing parse error two layers away from the actual fault.

The failure this is really aimed at
-----------------------------------
A total ML-layer failure used to return HTTP 200 on every route while `/health`
reported `"status": "online"`. Every model could be unavailable and nothing —
not a status code, not a log line an operator would notice, not a health check —
would say so. The dashboard simply rendered empty charts.

So `health_report()` inspects what actually loaded rather than whether a dataframe
key exists, and returns a degraded verdict that `/health` surfaces as a non-200.
A monitor pointed at `/health` now trips instead of going quiet.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/observability.py

chunks.text:
Pre-deploy preflight for AppSail.

Run this before `catalyst deploy --only appsail`:

    cd appsail && python predeploy_check.py

Why it exists
-------------
The two things AppSail needs most are both **gitignored**, so a clean checkout
looks complete and deploys "successfully" while the container refuses to start:

* `_vendor/` — Catalyst's managed Python runtime does **not** install
  `requirements.txt` server-side. Dependencies must be vendored into the build
  directory and placed on `PYTHONPATH`. Without it the container cannot import
  flask, and AppSail reports only:

      Execution failed. Please check the startup command or port.

  which says nothing about missing dependencies and sends you to inspect the
  startup command instead. This cost an afternoon of deploy cycles once —
  entrypoint form, memory tier, package size and the Dockerfile were each ruled
  out before the real cause surfaced.

* `app-config.json` — holds live API keys, so only `app-config.example.json` is
  committed. The real file drifts, and the drift that matters is the `command`
  losing its `PYTHONPATH=_vendor` prefix.

Exits non-zero on any hard failure so it can gate a deploy script.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/predeploy_check.py

chunks.text:
Keep person names off the wire to third-party LLM providers.

The problem
-----------
The copilot answers questions by injecting real records into the prompt — named
offenders with their rowdy-sheeter status and gang, the highest-risk individual on
the watchlist by name — and POSTs that prompt to Groq or NVIDIA. Those are
third-party services outside India. Sending citizen and offender PII to them is a
cross-border transfer that a police deployment cannot make casually, and until now
it happened on every copilot message.

The approach
------------
Alias on the way out, restore on the way back.

Names the platform injects are replaced with stable per-request aliases
(`[PERSON_1]`, `[PERSON_2]`) before the prompt leaves the process. The model
reasons over the aliases perfectly well — it only needs referential consistency,
not the actual name — and the aliases are mapped back to real names locally before
the answer is shown. The provider sees structure and never sees a person.

This keeps the feature genuinely useful, which matters: a redaction that makes the
copilot useless would simply be turned off.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/privacy.py

chunks.text:
Limits, stated plainly
----------------------
* A name the *user types themselves* is passed through. That is their own input,
  and rewriting a query mid-flight would break the search it describes. Set
  `LLM_BLOCK_TYPED_NAMES=1` to refuse such queries outright instead.
* Aliasing hides identity, not the attributes attached to it. "[PERSON_1], 44
  prior cases, operates across 20 districts" is still a detailed record, and in a
  small enough population that is re-identifiable. This reduces exposure; it does
  not make the transfer risk-free.
* **It only covers the call sites that use it.** A code review found three prompt
  paths still sending names raw — the most-connected suspects in the briefing,
  missing-person names, and officer name plus badge number — months after this
  module's docstring claimed the provider "never sees a person". Any new code that
  interpolates a name into a prompt must call `mask()`; there is no interception
  layer that will do it for you.
* The alias map lives only for the request that created it.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/privacy.py

chunks.text:
Replay the held-out test window through the serving path and the feedback loop.

Why this exists
---------------
`ml/outcomes.py` can measure whether predictions came true, and reports "no outcomes
recorded yet" because none have been — the platform has never been used against live
cases. That is honest, and it also means the single most important check in an ML
system has never actually run end to end.

The corpus already contains the answers for the held-out window: real recorded
verdicts and chargesheet dates the models were never trained on. Scoring that window
through the *serving* artifact and feeding the known results into the feedback loop
does two things a training run cannot:

1. **It detects training/serving skew.** Offline evaluation scores a model inside the
   training script, with the training script's own frame. Serving loads a joblib and
   scores a frame rebuilt elsewhere. Those two paths can diverge — a dropped column, a
   changed dtype, a different category encoding — and every symptom is silent: the
   model still returns numbers, they are just worse. Comparing the replayed metric
   against the published one is how that gets caught.
2. **It exercises the loop.** Prediction log, join, maturity window, base-rate
   baseline, calibration bands — none of it had ever run on real pairs.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/replay_outcomes.py

chunks.text:
What this is NOT
----------------
It is not evidence the system is in use, and it must never be read as field
performance. Every entry it writes carries `source="replay"`, `realised()` reports the
breakdown by source, and `/models/performance` shows it — so a replayed number can
never be mistaken for an operational one. The outcomes are real records from the
corpus; the *observation dates* are synthetic scaffolding, set to the score date plus
the model's own maturity window, because the loop needs a date and the corpus does not
always carry a resolution timestamp.

Preview by default, like the retention tooling: writing to the prediction and outcome
sinks is a real mutation of the runtime record.

    python replay_outcomes.py                      # preview both models
    python replay_outcomes.py --model conviction_outcome --apply
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/replay_outcomes.py

chunks.text:
Retention schedules and the erasure path.

Why this exists
---------------
Three runtime logs accumulate personal data indefinitely: who accessed whose record
(`audit.jsonl`), what score each person was given (`predictions.jsonl`), and what
happened to them (`outcomes.jsonl`). Under the DPDP Act 2023 personal data may be
kept only as long as the purpose requires, and a data principal may ask for erasure.
Neither was implemented, and "we never delete anything" is not a defensible answer
for a system holding police records.

The hard part: erasure conflicts with the audit chain
-----------------------------------------------------
The audit log is hash-chained precisely so that entries cannot be removed. Erasing a
person from it would break every digest after their entry — which is the chain
working correctly, not a bug to route around. Rewriting the chain to hide the removal
would defeat the entire control.

So the two are separated, and the reasoning is stated rather than hidden:
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/retention.py

chunks.text:
* **Prediction and outcome logs** hold *assessments of* a person. These are erased on
  request. They carry no chain, so rewriting them is sound.
* **The audit log** holds a record of *who looked at* a person — evidence of official
  conduct, not an assessment of the subject. It is not erased on request. It is
  bounded by a retention schedule instead, and enforced at whole-file granularity so
  the chain inside each file stays verifiable.

That distinction is the standard resolution, and it is the honest one: an access log
that a subject could delete would let anyone who improperly viewed a record erase the
proof by filing a request in the subject's name.

Every erasure is itself audited, naming what was erased and what deliberately was not.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/retention.py

chunks.text:
AppSail entrypoint.

Do **not** import `main` here.

`main` starts a background warm-up thread at import time (see the
`threading.Thread(target=_warmup...)` at the bottom of main.py) which builds the
full corpus, knowledge graph and models. So `from main import app` in this
parent process does not merely check that the app is importable — it loads
everything. `os.system` then starts gunicorn, which imports `main` a second time
and loads everything again, concurrently.

At 5,000 cases that was roughly 150 MB twice and fit inside the container. At
18,000 cases it is roughly 370 MB twice, the container is OOM-killed before
gunicorn can bind, and AppSail reports:

    Execution failed. Please check the startup command or port.

which says nothing about memory and sends you looking at the startup command.

So: no pre-import. This process holds nothing but the standard library, gunicorn
loads the app exactly once, and if that load fails the traceback is served rather
than left as an opaque 503.

One worker, threaded. The dataset, graph and fitted models live in module-level
state, so a second worker would be a second full copy. Concurrency comes from
threads sharing the one copy.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/run_gunicorn.py

chunks.text:
Criminological outcome simulator — a documented data-generating process.

Why this exists
---------------
The original generator assigned offenders to cases with `random.randint(1, n)` and
set trial results with `random.choice(["Convicted", "Acquitted", "Pending Trial"])`.
Under that process there is, by construction, no relationship between anything
observable and any outcome. When the models in `ml/` were evaluated properly for
the first time they returned ROC-AUC 0.47 for recidivism and 0.52 for case
progression — correct measurements of a world containing no signal.

Rather than hide that behind a random train/test split, this script replaces the
outcome tables with a simulation that has explicit, documented structure. Every
coefficient below is a stated assumption, and the models are given only
*observable* consequences — never the latent variables themselves.

READ THIS BEFORE QUOTING ANY METRIC
-----------------------------------
This is simulated data with a known ground truth. A model scoring well here has
demonstrated that it can *recover a known structure* — which is the correct thing
to verify before real data exists, and is genuinely informative about whether the
pipeline, the features and the validation are sound. It is NOT evidence of field
performance on real KSP records, and the model registry says so on every card.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/simulate_outcomes.py

chunks.text:
The data-generating process
---------------------------
**Offenders.** Each of the N offenders draws latent traits, none of which are ever
given to a model:
  lambda   offending rate per active year, LogNormal(mu=-0.9, sigma=1.3), 0.05-8.0
           (heavy-tailed: most offenders appear once or twice, a few dominate)
  crew     ~65% belong to one of the crews; crews drive co-offending and gangs
  speciality  a preferred crime type, weighted by the +3.0 term below
  home     a home district, weighted by the +1.2 term below
           (the realised adherence rates are measured and printed on every run,
            rather than asserted here)
  onset    career start date, uniform over the corpus span
  career   career length, Exponential(mean 2.6y), so some offenders desist

**Case attribution.** For each case in date order, 1-3 offenders are drawn with
probability proportional to exp(score), where
    score = log(lambda) + 3.0*speciality_match + 1.2*home_district_match
            + 0.8*active_at_incident_date
and additional accused are drawn from the first accused's crew with p=0.72. This
produces genuine repeat offending, genuine specialisation and genuine co-offending
communities — the structures the recidivism model, the community detection and the
link prediction are all supposed to find.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/simulate_outcomes.py

chunks.text:
**Arrest.** P(arrest) = sigmoid(-0.9 + 0.34*z(witnesses) + 0.42*z(severity)
    + 0.55*z(prior cases) + 0.30*rowdy_sheeter). Delay ~ Gamma(k=2, theta=12 days),
stretched by station load.

**Chargesheet.** Filed for 88% of cases with at least one arrest. Delay ~
Gamma(k=2.4) with a mean that grows with the number of accused, case severity and
the station's 90-day load, and shrinks with the investigating officer's experience.
The `case_closure` model's target — chargesheet within 180 days — is therefore a
real consequence of case complexity and station capacity.

**Conviction.** For chargesheeted cases,
    P(convict) = sigmoid(-0.35 + 0.30*z(witnesses) - 0.45*z(arrest delay)
        - 0.35*z(chargesheet delay) + 0.25*z(severity) + 0.20*z(prior cases)
        - 0.22*z(co-accused count))
i.e. convictions follow evidence quality and investigative promptness. Cases whose
chargesheet is recent are left 'Pending Trial'.

**Registry consistency.** past_fir_count and past_arrests in CriminalsRegistry are
recomputed from the simulated event tables. In the original data they were
independent random draws that contradicted the case records — which is also why
they had to be banned as features.

Deterministic (seeded). Run:  python simulate_outcomes.py [--dry-run]
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/simulate_outcomes.py

chunks.text:
KSP IntelHub machine-learning package.

Everything that fits, validates or scores a model lives here. The Flask app
(`main.py`) only *consumes* this package — it never defines features or metrics
itself, so the numbers shown in the UI are exactly the numbers produced by the
offline training run.

Layout
------
config.py     constants, paths, feature specs, evaluation policy
dataset.py    the adapter: raw tables -> canonical frames (the real-data swap point)
splits.py     temporal / grouped / walk-forward splitters
baselines.py  the "can a trivial rule do this?" reference models
evaluate.py   honest metric computation (incl. confusion, calibration, lift)
registry.py   artifact persistence + the portable JSON evaluation report
tasks/        one module per model, each exposing train(...) -> TrainedModel
train.py      CLI entrypoint:  python -m ml.train
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/__init__.py

chunks.text:
Baselines — the "could a trivial rule do this?" reference models.

An accuracy figure means nothing on its own. 82% sounds strong until you learn
that always guessing the majority class scores 79%. Every model in this package
is reported next to the baselines here, and the honest headline number is the
*lift over baseline*, not the raw score.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/baselines.py

chunks.text:
Central configuration for the ML layer.

Anything a reviewer might want to challenge — split dates, horizons, which
features are banned as leaky — is declared here rather than buried in model code.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/config.py

chunks.text:
Adapter layer: raw tables on disk -> canonical dataframes the models consume.

This is the ONLY module that knows the physical schema. Every model downstream
speaks the canonical vocabulary defined below. To train on real KSP extracts,
point `load_canonical` at the new directory and adjust the mapping functions
here — no model, metric or endpoint changes.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/dataset.py

chunks.text:
Canonical frames
----------------
cases      one row per FIR         case_id, case_key, district, police_station,
                                   crime_type, ts, severity_score, status,
                                   latitude, longitude, weapon_used, vehicle_used,
                                   target_type, officer_id, witnesses, fatalities,
                                   injured, accused_count
reports    one row per narrative   case_id, report_text, officer_id
offenders  one row per person      offender_id, name, past_fir_count, past_arrests,
                                   rowdy_sheeter, history_sheet, active_warrant,
                                   gang_affiliation, risk_level, known_associates
accused    person <-> case         case_key, offender_id, age, gender
courts     one row per trial       case_key, chargesheet_status, conviction_status,
                                   court_name, next_hearing
officers   one row per officer     officer_id, rank, station, district,
                                   specialization, appointment_date, ...
arrests    one row per arrest      case_key, arrest_date, offender_id
socio      one row per district    district + indicator columns
links      case <-> suspect        case_id, suspect_id, relationship
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/dataset.py

chunks.text:
Metric computation.

One place produces every number the UI shows. Rules this module enforces:

* accuracy is never reported alone — it always ships with a baseline to compare against;
* probabilistic models are scored for *calibration* (Brier, reliability bins), not just
  ranking, because "72% likely to reoffend" is a claim about frequency and a
  miscalibrated score is actively misleading in a policing context;
* multi-class results carry a full confusion matrix and per-class support, so a
  class the model never gets right cannot hide inside a macro average.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/evaluate.py

chunks.text:
Runtime model monitoring: what the models are actually doing once deployed.

The offline evaluation in this package is strong — temporal splits, baselines,
calibration, leakage probes. All of it describes the models on the day they were
trained. Nothing described them afterwards.

That gap matters more here than the offline rigour does. A model trained on a
corpus where 42% of prosecutions ended in conviction, running two years later
against a district where filing practice has changed, will keep returning
confident probabilities and nothing in the system would notice. The registry
could not even tell you what it had predicted last week.

Three things live here:

**Prediction logging.** Every score the platform hands to a person is recorded —
model, subject, value, and the time. This is the raw material for everything
else: without a record of what was predicted, "was it right?" is unanswerable
and no feedback loop can ever be built.

**Reference profiles.** At training time each model stores the distribution of
its own input features and output scores. That is the baseline drift is measured
against, and it has to be captured then — reconstructing it later from a corpus
that has already moved is circular.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/monitoring.py

chunks.text:
**Drift detection** via Population Stability Index, the standard measure in
credit risk for exactly this question. PSI compares a current distribution
against the reference:

    < 0.10   stable
    0.10-0.25  moderate shift, worth watching
    > 0.25   significant shift, the model is being asked about a different
             population than the one it learned

PSI is reported per feature and for the score distribution. It detects that the
inputs moved; it cannot tell you the model got worse, because that needs
outcomes, and outcomes need the feedback loop this file's prediction log is the
first half of. Stated plainly rather than implied.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/monitoring.py

chunks.text:
Record what actually happened to the people the models scored.

Why this exists
---------------
Everything else in the ML layer measures the models against history. Offline
evaluation says how they did on a held-out slice of the past; drift monitoring says
whether today's inputs still look like that past. Neither can answer the only
question that matters once the system is in use: *are the answers still right?*

Drift is not a proxy for it. Inputs can stay perfectly stable while a model's
accuracy collapses — a change in charging practice, a new court, a shift in what
gets recorded — and PSI will read `stable` throughout. The reverse is just as
common: inputs move because the world moved, and the model is fine.

The only way to answer it is to write down what the prediction was, wait, and then
write down what happened. This module is that second half.

Shape
-----
Two append-only logs, joined on `(model, subject_id)`:

  predictions.jsonl   written by `monitoring.log_prediction` at serving time
  outcomes.jsonl      written here when someone records a real result

`realised(model)` joins them and reports measured performance against the metric the
registry published at training time. A gap between the two is the signal that
offline evaluation has stopped describing reality.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/outcomes.py

chunks.text:
What this does not do
---------------------
It does not make outcomes appear. Until real results are recorded the join is empty
and every function here says so rather than returning a comfortable zero. An empty
feedback loop is still better than none: it is the difference between "we have not
measured this" and "we cannot".
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/outcomes.py

chunks.text:
Model registry — artifact persistence and the portable evaluation report.

Two separate concerns, deliberately kept separate:

1. **Artifacts** (`*.joblib`) are a *speed* optimisation. They are pickled
   estimators, so they are only loadable by a compatible scikit-learn build.
   If the runtime differs from the training machine, loading is refused and the
   caller retrains in-process from the same code path. Nothing breaks; boot is
   just slower.

2. **The report** (`model_registry.json`) is the *evidence*. Pure JSON, portable
   everywhere, committed to the repo. It is what the UI renders and what a judge
   reads. It is never regenerated at request time, so the metrics on screen are
   always the ones produced by a real, reproducible training run.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/registry.py

chunks.text:
Serving layer — what the Flask app calls at boot.

Load order for every model:

1. Try the persisted artifact. This is the fast path (a few hundred milliseconds
   for the whole set) and it guarantees the served model is byte-identical to the
   one the published metrics were measured on.
2. If the artifact is absent, or was built by a different scikit-learn version,
   retrain in-process from the *same* task module. Slower, but the two paths run
   identical code, so they cannot disagree about what a model is.

Metrics are never recomputed here. They are read from `model_registry.json`,
which is written only by an offline training run. That is deliberate: a metric
computed at request time against whatever data happens to be loaded is not a
measurement, and the number on the dashboard should be the number somebody can
reproduce by re-running the trainer.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/serving.py

chunks.text:
Splitters.

Crime records are events on a timeline. A random `train_test_split` lets a model
learn from cases registered *after* the ones it is scored on, which quietly
inflates every metric — the model gets to see the future. Every supervised task
in this package uses one of the splitters below instead.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/splits.py

chunks.text:
Survival-analysis primitives — the right tool for "how long until X?".

Why this module exists
----------------------
`tasks/allocation.py` asks a binary question: *was a chargesheet filed within 180
days?* To ask it honestly it has to throw away every case registered in the last
180 days of the corpus, because those cases have not had time to answer. On this
dataset that discards the most recent — and most operationally relevant — cases,
and it still cannot say anything at all about a case that is open **right now**.

That discarded information has a name: **right-censoring**. A case registered 40
days ago with no chargesheet has not "failed"; it is simply still running. It
carries real evidence — *this case survived at least 40 days* — and survival
analysis is the branch of statistics built to use it.

Treating censored rows as negatives biases the model toward pessimism; dropping
them biases it toward whatever was true further in the past. Neither is
acceptable when the output is "which of my open cases will breach the SLA".

Approach: discrete-time survival
--------------------------------
Rather than take a dependency on `lifelines` or `scikit-survival`, this module
uses **discrete-time survival analysis via person-period expansion**, which needs
nothing beyond the scikit-learn already in `requirements.txt` and is a standard,
textbook-correct construction:
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/survival.py

chunks.text:
1. Chop follow-up into fixed intervals (here, 30-day months).
2. Expand each case into one row per interval it *survived into* — stopping at
   the interval where the chargesheet lands, or at censoring.
3. Fit a plain classifier on those rows. Because each row asks "given this case
   reached interval k, did the event happen *in* interval k?", the fitted
   probability is exactly the **discrete hazard** h(k | x).
4. Recover the survival curve by chaining: S(t | x) = prod_{k<=t} (1 - h(k | x)).

Censored cases contribute every interval they survived and simply stop — they are
never scored as failures. That is the whole point.

This construction also buys something the binary model structurally cannot give:
one fitted model answers *every* horizon. The 60-day, 90-day and 180-day SLA
questions all read off the same curve, instead of needing three separate models
that could disagree with each other.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/survival.py

chunks.text:
Offline training entrypoint.

    python -m ml.train                 # train everything, write artifacts + report
    python -m ml.train --only narrative_classifier recidivism_risk
    python -m ml.train --no-artifacts  # evaluate and report, persist nothing
    python -m ml.train --data-dir ../real_extract

Produces:
    artifacts/<model>.joblib      fitted estimators (a boot-time speed path)
    artifacts/model_registry.json the portable evaluation report the UI renders

The report is the deliverable. Artifacts are an optimisation: if the serving
runtime has a different scikit-learn build they are refused on load and the app
retrains in-process from this same code, so the two paths can never disagree
about what a model is.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/train.py

chunks.text:
One module per model.

Every task module exposes the same two functions so `train.py` and `main.py`
can treat them uniformly:

    train(data, report) -> artifact        fits, evaluates, records into the report
    make_predictor(artifact) -> callable   rebuilds the live scoring function

`artifact` is a plain dict that joblib can persist. It always carries an `_env`
key stamped by the registry so a mismatched runtime is detected on load rather
than producing silently wrong scores.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/__init__.py

chunks.text:
Case progression — will this FIR reach a chargesheet within 180 days?

Two things were wrong with the previous version of this model.

**Target leakage.** It fed the investigating officer's `closure_rate`,
`cases_assigned` and `commendations` into a model predicting whether a case
closed. Those columns are aggregates *computed from case outcomes*, including
the outcome of the very case being scored — the label was sitting inside the
features. All three are banned in `config.BANNED_ALLOCATION_FEATURES` and the
model is rebuilt from case facts and officer attributes that exist before the
investigation starts.

**An undefined target.** `status == 'Closed'` is a snapshot with no clock. A case
registered in 2020 has had six years to close; one registered last month has had
weeks. Comparing them measures the calendar, not the investigation. Since a
random split scatters both across train and test, the old accuracy figure was
largely a reading of case age.

Here the target is explicitly time-boxed: **was a chargesheet filed within 180
days of registration?** ChargesheetDetails carries real dates, so the outcome is
observable, and cases too recent for the full 180 days to have elapsed are
excluded rather than counted as failures.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/allocation.py

chunks.text:
Trial outcome — will a named accused be convicted?

Used to help prosecutors and IOs see which pending trials look evidentially weak
early enough to strengthen them.

This is the model in the platform that most needs guard rails, so it carries the
most:

* **Grouped temporal split.** Rows are split so that no individual appears in
  both halves *and* the test half is later in time. Without the grouping, a
  prolific offender with eight cases seeds both sides and the model is scored
  partly on how well it memorised that person.
* **No snapshot registry flags.** `rowdy_sheeter`, `history_sheet` and
  `active_warrant` are undated current-state columns; a warrant recorded today
  may well be a consequence of the very conviction being predicted. Prior history
  is recomputed from dated case and arrest records instead.
* **Calibration reported.** A number shown next to a person's name as a
  likelihood of conviction has to mean what it says, so Brier score and a
  reliability curve are part of the headline, not an appendix.
* **Fairness slices.** Accuracy is broken out by age band and gender so a model
  that works well overall but poorly for one group cannot pass unnoticed.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/conviction.py

chunks.text:
Weekly incident-volume forecasting.

Ridge regression on a linear trend plus Fourier seasonality terms (annual,
semi-annual, quarterly), fitted state-wide, per district and per crime type.

What changed versus a plain "fit and plot" forecaster
----------------------------------------------------
1. **Walk-forward backtest.** The model is re-fitted at several historical
   origins and scored only on weeks after each origin — the way a forecast would
   actually have been issued. A single in-sample fit tells you nothing about
   forecast skill.
2. **Reported against baselines.** Naive, seasonal-naive, moving-average and
   drift forecasts are backtested identically. The headline is MASE: below 1.0
   the model beats the naive forecast, at or above 1.0 it does not — and if it
   does not, the report says so.
3. **Honest prediction intervals.** The interval width is derived from
   *out-of-sample backtest residuals at each horizon step*, not from in-sample
   residuals. In-sample residuals are systematically too small and produce
   intervals that look tight and cover far less than they claim. Realised
   coverage is measured and reported next to the nominal 80%.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/forecast.py

chunks.text:
Geospatial hotspot zones — DBSCAN over incident coordinates (haversine).

The previous version hard-coded `eps_km=45, min_samples=3` with no justification.
45 km is a very large radius for a "hotspot" — at that scale a cluster spans most
of a district and tells a patrol commander nothing actionable.

Here the parameters are **selected**, not assumed: a grid of (eps, min_samples)
is scored on silhouette (cluster separation), the share of points left as noise,
and whether the resulting zones are small enough to actually patrol. The chosen
setting and the full sweep are both written to the report, so the choice is
auditable rather than asserted.

DBSCAN has no ground truth to validate against, so these are internal validity
measures. They are reported as such — this is unsupervised structure discovery,
not prediction, and the report says so explicitly.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/hotspots.py

chunks.text:
FIR narrative -> crime type.

Reads the free-text body of a First Information Report and predicts which crime
head it belongs to, so that un-categorised or mis-categorised reports can be
triaged automatically.

What makes this evaluation trustworthy
--------------------------------------
* **Temporal split.** Scored only on FIRs registered after the cutoff date.
* **Leakage scrub.** The structured [METADATA:] tag and any legal-section line
  are stripped before the text reaches the vectoriser, and a probe (below)
  checks that no single token is a perfect give-away for a class.
* **Baselines.** Reported against majority-class and stratified-random, because
  accuracy without a reference point is not a result.
* **Model selection on the training window only.** Hyper-parameters are chosen
  by cross-validation *inside* the training period; the test window is touched
  exactly once, at the end.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/narrative.py

chunks.text:
Case pendency — how long until this FIR reaches a chargesheet?

This is the survival-analysis counterpart to `allocation.py`, and it exists
because the binary model has two limits that no amount of tuning removes.

**It discards the cases you most need scored.** To ask "chargesheet within 180
days?" honestly, `allocation.py` must drop every case registered in the final 180
days of the corpus — they have not had time to answer. Those are precisely the
cases sitting open on a desk today. The model is structurally incapable of
scoring the live docket.

**It answers one question forever.** SCRB does not have a single 180-day clock.
Different offence classes carry different statutory and administrative
expectations, and a Superintendent wants the 60-day figure while a court-liaison
cell wants 180. Three binary models would be three chances to disagree.

Modelling time-to-event fixes both. A case open 40 days with no chargesheet is
**right-censored**, not a failure: it tells us "survived at least 40 days", and
survival analysis is built to use exactly that. One fitted model then answers
every horizon off a single curve.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/pendency.py

chunks.text:
Construction
------------
Discrete-time survival via person-period expansion (see `ml/survival.py`) —
sklearn-only, no new dependency. Each case becomes one row per 30-day interval it
survived into; a classifier on those rows *is* an estimator of the discrete
hazard h(k | x); chaining gives S(t | x).

Guard rails carried over from `allocation.py`, because they apply identically:

* The banned officer aggregates (`closure_rate`, `cases_assigned`,
  `commendations`) stay banned — they are computed from case outcomes and
  contain the label.
* Split is temporal on registration date.
* Station workload is measured in the 90 days *before* registration.

Baseline: the **Kaplan-Meier** curve. It is the covariate-free answer — what you
can say about a case knowing only that it exists — and it is the reference a
survival model has to beat to have learned anything at all.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/pendency.py

chunks.text:
Recidivism risk — will this offender be named in a new case within a year?

The platform previously reported a "recidivism risk index" that was a hand-weighted
sum of registry flags (30 x prior offences + 20 x arrests + 20 x risk level ...).
That is a scoring rubric, not a model: nothing in it was ever fitted to, or tested
against, an observed outcome, so there was no way to know whether a score of 78
meant anything different from a score of 45.

This module defines an actual supervised target and measures it.

Target
------
Fix an observation date T. Using only records dated before T, describe each
offender. Then look at the window (T, T + 365 days] and label 1 if they are named
in a *new* case during it. The label is therefore always in the future relative
to every feature.

Two disjoint panels
-------------------
Training uses T_train, testing uses T_test = T_train + 365 days, so the training
outcome window closes exactly where the test window opens. No outcome is ever
shared between the two, and no feature is computed from a period the model is
later scored on.
chunks.title: Backend module appsail/ml/tasks/recidivism.py

chunks.text:
Leakage controls
----------------
* `past_fir_count` / `past_arrests` from CriminalsRegistry are **excluded**. They
  are current-state snapshot columns with no as-of date, so they may well count
  offences committed after T — which is the label. Equivalent counts are
  recomputed from the dated case and arrest tables instead.
* The snapshot boolean flags (rowdy sheeter, history sheet, active warrant) have
  the same problem. The headline model omits them; an ablation that includes them
  is reported alongside, and the gap between the two is exactly the size of the
  optimism those columns would have introduced.
* The old hand-weighted index is scored as a baseline, so "does the learned model
  actually beat the rubric we had?" is answered with a number.
